summaries.example: Imagine a card that says, “What this card says is not true.” If the card is telling the truth, then its message is not true. But if its message is not true, then the card seems to be telling the truth. The card keeps switching between the two choices.
summaries.summary: The Liar paradox is a family of puzzles about truth. A simple version says, “This sentence is not true.” If it is true, what it says makes it not true. If it is not true, then what it says appears to make it true. That circular reasoning seems to produce a contradiction. Other versions use two sentences that refer to each other, an endless line of sentences, or a sentence with an “or.” The puzzle is not mainly about whether someone intends to deceive. It is about how truth works. Philosophers have suggested several kinds of answers. Some say that certain sentences are neither true nor false. Some allow a sentence to be both true and false but reject the rule that a contradiction proves everything. Others limit how a truth word can be used, or say that meaning can change with context. No single solution is presented as settled in the source.
key_ideas: The Liar paradox begins when a sentence talks about its own truth or falsehood.
A sentence that says “I am not true” seems to be true and not true at the same time.
Similar puzzles can use two people’s statements, a longer group of statements, or more complicated words such as “or.”
Philosophers and logicians disagree about which rule about truth or logic should be changed.
Some proposed answers use a third status besides true and false; others allow a contradiction without letting every statement become true.
summaries.why_it_matters: The puzzle shows that ordinary-looking ideas about truth and logic can interact in surprising ways. It has helped philosophers study self-reference, language, and different systems of reasoning. It also teaches an important thinking habit: when an argument reaches an impossible result, examine which starting rules made the result possible.

important_terms.definition: A puzzle in which careful-looking reasoning seems to lead to a contradiction or an impossible result.
When a sentence, statement, or object refers to itself. For example, a sentence talks about that very sentence.
The quality of matching how things are. A true sentence says things that are the case.
A statement that says something is not true. In these puzzles, this can create trouble when the statement refers to itself.

questions_to_think_about: Can a sentence safely describe its own truth?
If a statement is neither true nor false, what kind of status does it have?
Should one contradiction make every statement acceptable?
Does a puzzle have to use one sentence talking about itself?

summaries.example: Let L be the sentence “L is not true.” Suppose classical logic gives every sentence one of two statuses: true or false. If L is true, then its content makes L not true. If L is not true, capture of that content makes L true. Thus L appears to be both true and not true. If contradictions imply every sentence, the system becomes trivial: it can establish any claim, even an unrelated one.
summaries.summary: The Liar paradox concerns sentences whose semantic content turns back on truth itself. The simple-untruth form says of itself that it is not true; the simple-falsity form says of itself that it is false. Under familiar assumptions, each yields a contradiction. The same pattern can arise without direct self-reference: two claims can form a cycle, as when one says the other is true and the other says the first is not true. More complex constructions use disjunctions, and an infinite sequence associated with Yablo raises the question of whether circularity is essential. The abstract mechanism combines a truth predicate with principles often described as capture and release: from A one may infer that A is true, and from “A is true” one may infer A. Classical principles such as excluded middle and explosion then make the contradiction disastrous. Proposed responses divide broadly. Paracomplete logics allow gaps; paraconsistent logics allow some gluts without triviality; substructural logics revise rules governing the use of premises; classical approaches restrict truth through hierarchies, grounding, or partial constructions; contextualist approaches make semantic status depend on context; revision theory treats truth as governed by a process that may fail to stabilize. The entry emphasizes that each family has motivations and unresolved challenges.
key_ideas: The Liar is a family, not just one sentence: it includes direct self-reference, cycles between sentences, Boolean compounds, and proposed non-circular infinite sequences.

The paradox depends on several ingredients: a truth predicate, enough expressive power for self-reference, principles connecting a sentence with its truth claim, and logical rules such as excluded middle or explosion.
Paracomplete theories preserve strong truth principles by allowing truth-value gaps, while paraconsistent theories may allow gluts—sentences that are both true and false—while rejecting explosion.
Other approaches change structural features of consequence, restrict truth to a hierarchy or grounded sentences, make truth context-sensitive, or revise interpretations over time.
A proposed solution can face a revenge problem: a new sentence may describe the proposed solution and recreate a related paradox.
The source presents these approaches as an active philosophical disagreement rather than a single settled resolution.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Liar tests the relationship among language, truth, and logical consequence. It has influenced debates about whether classical logic is appropriate for semantic reasoning, whether truth is vague or context-dependent, and whether a language can describe its own semantic behavior. More technically, it shows how apparently modest principles can produce triviality when combined. Studying the paradox therefore helps clarify what a logical system permits, what a truth predicate means, and where a proposed solution may need further restrictions.

important_terms.definition: A family of arguments in which ordinary principles about truth and logic appear to generate contradiction or triviality.
A predicate used to say that a sentence or other truth-bearer is true; the source uses Tr as a formal symbol for it.
The principle that every sentence is either true or false. Rejecting it can produce a gap between truth and falsity.
The rule that a sentence and its negation together imply any sentence. Rejecting this rule is central to paraconsistent approaches.
The pattern linking a sentence A with “A is true,” often expressed as a biconditional. It guides capture and release.
A logic in which some sentences may be neither true nor false; it blocks certain classical inferences such as excluded middle.
A logic that can tolerate some contradictions without allowing every sentence to follow from them.
A sentence or process that never settles on a stable truth status. Revision theories use this idea for the Liar.

questions_to_think_about: Is it more plausible to reject bivalence, reject explosion, restrict the truth predicate, or revise another logical rule?
Can a language contain a truth predicate that applies to its own sentences without becoming paradoxical?
Does a paracomplete solution adequately describe a Liar as neither true nor false if it cannot express that description itself?
Would a contextual shift explain the Liar, or merely move the difficulty to a new level?
Does an infinite sequence avoid self-reference, or does its structure still create a kind of circular dependence?

summaries.example: Maya writes: “Jordan’s next sentence is true.” Jordan replies: “Maya’s sentence is not true.” If Maya’s sentence is true exactly when Jordan’s is true, while Jordan’s is true exactly when Maya’s is not true, the two claims force one statement to be true just when it is not true. The problem does not depend on either student lying on purpose; it comes from the pattern of their claims.
summaries.summary: The Liar paradox begins with a sentence such as “This sentence is not true.” If the sentence is true, its own content says that it is not true. If it is not true, the content seems to make it true. This creates a contradiction, and in many familiar logical systems a contradiction leads to triviality, where every statement can be derived. The source treats the Liar as a wider family. Two sentences can refer to each other in a cycle, a sentence can contain a more complicated “or” structure, and an infinite series can produce a related problem without obvious direct self-reference. The common ingredients include a truth predicate and rules connecting a sentence to its being true. Philosophers disagree about which ingredient should be revised. Paracomplete approaches deny that every sentence is true or false. Paraconsistent approaches accept that some sentences may be both true and false but deny that contradictions prove everything. Substructural approaches change rules about how premises may be reused or combined. Classical approaches keep ordinary logic but restrict the truth predicate, perhaps by using separate language levels or by distinguishing grounded from problematic sentences. Contextualist theories connect the issue to changing contexts, while revision theories describe truth through repeated attempts to settle its extension. The entry surveys these options without claiming that one answer has won.
key_ideas: The Liar paradox is a group of related puzzles about sentences that concern their own truth or falsehood.
Direct self-reference is not required: cycles between different speakers can create the same pattern, and an infinite sequence may appear to avoid circularity.
The trouble comes from combining truth rules with logical assumptions such as bivalence and explosion.
One response rejects excluded middle for problematic sentences, creating a gap between true and false.
Another response accepts contradictions but rejects explosion, so the system does not collapse into the result that every statement is true.

Other philosophers preserve classical logic by restricting truth to certain languages, grounded sentences, or contexts; these proposals face questions about whether the restrictions are natural and whether new “revenge” puzzles arise.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Liar is important because it reveals that “truth” is not a harmless notion when a language can talk about its own sentences. It connects elementary puzzles with major issues in logic and philosophy of language: self-reference, the limits of formal systems, the behavior of negation and implication, and the expressive power of a language. It also provides a way to compare theories: a good proposal must explain the paradox while avoiding an unacceptable collapse or an equally troubling replacement puzzle.

important_terms.definition: A puzzling argument whose apparently reasonable steps seem to produce a contradiction or an absurd conclusion.
A statement that refers to itself, directly or through another statement or object.
A word or idea used to describe whether a sentence matches the facts or says what is the case.
The assumption that every sentence must be either true or false, with no third option.
A formal way to connect a sentence with the claim that the sentence is true, roughly saying “A is true if and only if A.”
A logic that allows some claims to fall between true and false rather than forcing a yes-or-no answer.
A logic that can contain some true-and-false claims without allowing one contradiction to prove everything.

questions_to_think_about: Does a sentence need to refer to itself directly for a Liar paradox to occur?
Which seems less costly: allowing a third truth status or allowing some contradictions?
Why might a hierarchy of languages prevent a Liar sentence from being well-formed?
If a solution cannot describe its own treatment of the Liar, is that a serious weakness?
Could changing the context change the status of a puzzling sentence?
